**Authors:** Ilana M. Umansky, Janette D. Avelar, and Karen D. Thompson  
**Venue:** American Educational Research Journal, 2026. DOI: 10.3102/00028312261453523  
**Review Date:** 2026-09-25  
**Model:** GPT-6 via Codex  
**Review Mode:** Retrospective (Reader’s Guide)

### Overall Assessment: Useful With Caveats

This paper provides useful statewide descriptive evidence about secondary students classified as English learners (ELs) in Oregon: fuller overall schedules can coexist with limited access to core coursework (Table 2, pp. 20–21). Its strongest contribution is the distinction between total enrolled credits and core-content opportunity, supported by a broad literature framing and linked administrative records. The preferred achievement models show small contemporaneous associations, while the graduation comparisons provide exploratory evidence about diploma type (Tables 7–8, pp. 29–31). My judgment is that neither the course-access regressions nor the graduation analysis establishes the effects of a defined expansion of instructional time: subject-credit outcomes are components of the enrollment-based exposure, and accumulated high-school exposure remains entangled with persistence and diploma plans. Reporting inconsistencies and unavailable diagnostic and replication materials further limit verification. These problems justify the methods, writing, and reproducibility reviews’ reservations without negating the descriptive contribution recognized by the literature and contribution reviews. Cite the paper selectively for relative course-enrollment patterns and hypothesis-generating outcome associations; do not treat its headline graduation claim as an established policy effect.

#### Key Strengths

- The statewide administrative records make ordinary course scheduling visible beyond individual named programs, with a locally relevant non-EL comparison group and separate measures of total and core enrollment (pp. 9, 12; Table 2, pp. 20–21). This is the paper’s most defensible scholarly contribution.
- Distinguishing course access, standardized achievement, and diploma type exposes outcomes that a test-score-only evaluation would miss (Tables 6–8, pp. 28–31). The distinction between fuller schedules and additional core instruction is substantively useful even without a causal interpretation.
- The literature review connects instructional-time research with curricular inequality and multilingual students’ broader educational opportunities; the paper also recognizes instructional quality, program context, and nonacademic benefits (pp. 3–8, 34–36). Its contribution is best understood as broadening the scope of the existing literature, not establishing that additional instruction can matter for the first time.
- Student fixed effects, observed-covariate matching, sequential specifications, and explicit limitations improve interpretability over raw outcome comparisons. The authors explain the outcome-switching restriction for full-load models and acknowledge changing confounders, incomplete course records, and unobserved credit completion and instructional quality (pp. 16–18, 36–37; Table 6 note, p. 28).

#### Key Concerns

- The exposure measures enrolled credits relative to peers, not observed instructional minutes or assignment to a common intervention. Subject-credit outcomes are themselves components of the total-credit predictor; full-load status summarizes the same schedule. My methodological judgment is that the positive course-taking coefficients describe enrollment composition more securely than they identify an independent causal effect on access (pp. 12, 14, 16; Table 6, p. 28).
- Graduation exposure accumulates during high school, allowing continued enrollment and diploma-track choices to influence both treatment classification and outcomes. Some instructional controls also accumulate after entry. Matching cannot establish that these pathways are removed; their importance is an identification concern, not an empirically measured bias in this review (pp. 17–18, 33–36; Table 8, pp. 30–31).
- Achievement estimates remain vulnerable to changing student circumstances, selection through continued EL classification, and assessment comparability. The current-EL panel and entry-defined graduation cohort cover different populations, so their results do not constitute a single causal trajectory from more coursework to graduation (pp. 9, 13, 16–18; Tables 7–8, pp. 29–31).
- The headline wording is stronger than the supported interpretation: the abstract says extra time ‘substantially increased the likelihood’ of full-course enrollment and regular-diploma graduation (p. 1), whereas the graduation section states ‘We consider these results exploratory’ (p. 29). Reporting errors add a separate obstacle: the narrative prints ‘OR = 0.0464’ (p. 32), while the corresponding table cell is ‘0.464’ (Table 8, p. 30). These are verified reporting problems, not proof that the underlying estimation was incorrect.
- The supplied article does not provide replication code or a documented data-access route, and important matching diagnostics, assessment harmonization, alternative estimates, and combined-diploma results are deferred to online appendices that are not bound into the PDF (pp. 9, 13, 17–18, 29, 32, 37–38). Sample and specification inconsistencies also obstruct exact reconstruction, as detailed in the verification notes. This assessment concerns the available report; it does not establish that no additional materials exist elsewhere.

#### What to Rely On

- Recorded core-course enrollment falls below the local non-EL benchmark on average: Table 2 reports a −0.21 core-credit differential alongside a −0.02 total-credit differential (p. 20). These are descriptive student-year averages, not causal effects or national estimates.
- Additional overall enrollment does not necessarily mean substantially greater core-content access: Table 2 reports extra total enrollment in approximately 18% of EL student-year observations; within that group, the average differentials are 0.96 total credits and 0.06 core credits (pp. 20–21). The prevalence applies to student-years under the paper’s relative-credit rule, not distinct students offered a supplemental program.
- The preferred achievement associations are small: per additional credit of differential, the core-credit ELA coefficient is 0.022 SD (SE 0.008), while the any-credit ELA coefficient is 0.012 and the any- and core-credit math coefficients are 0.002 and 0.010, respectively (all SEs 0.008; Table 7, p. 29). Only the core-credit ELA estimate is statistically significant in the preferred specification; this is evidence about measured outcomes in the observed panel.
- The study supplies exploratory matched evidence connecting extra enrollment with diploma type: the fully adjusted regular-diploma odds ratios are 1.133 for any extra time at the four-year horizon (no significance marker), 1.464 for core extra time at that horizon (p < .1), and 1.792 for any extra time at the five-year horizon (p < .05; Table 8, p. 30; legend, p. 31). This mixed pattern supports further investigation, not a uniform graduation benefit.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- Claims that externally increasing instructional time causes better course access: the enrollment exposure and course-taking outcomes overlap arithmetically, and fixed effects do not remove that overlap. The full-load results are odds ratios among students whose full-load status changes, not population-wide probability gains (pp. 12, 16; Table 6 and note, p. 28).
- Claims that extra time raises overall high-school completion or moves particular students from modified to regular diplomas: treatment timing and persistence remain unresolved, and diploma-specific models use different samples (pp. 17–18; Table 8, pp. 30–31). The authors report no statistically significant combined-diploma result on p. 32, citing unavailable Supplementary Appendix Table A7; that statement is author-reported, not independently verified here.
- Claims about the size of modified-diploma benefits: the narrative’s ‘54% lower’ and ‘OR = 0.0464’ (p. 32) conflict internally; Table 8 reports ‘0.464’ (p. 30), implying 53.6% lower odds. Likewise, ‘88% lower’ (p. 32) is inconsistent with the table’s ‘0.175’ (p. 31), which implies 82.5% lower odds. The continuation is headed ‘Four-year outcomes’ (p. 31), while the narrative calls that estimate ‘after 5 years’ (p. 32); the intended horizon remains unresolved in the supplied document.
- Claims that longer school days, summer programs, or online instruction are proven effective or cost-effective: the longer-day category is inferred from credit enrollment and the absence of other recorded formats, while summer and online records are incomplete. The paper neither isolates comparable interventions nor estimates their comparative costs (Table 4 and note, p. 24; pp. 33–37). Generalization beyond comparable Oregon course-enrollment settings also requires additional evidence.
- Claims that small test-score associations establish no learning benefit or diagnose poor instruction: test scores are separate from credit completion, broader educational outcomes, and instructional quality, which this design cannot jointly establish (Table 7, p. 29; pp. 35–37). Evidence about specific time interventions in the literature should not be treated as interchangeable with this relative-credit exposure.

#### Verification notes

Page citations refer to the article’s printed pages. The full supplied article was read, and central numerical exhibits were also checked in rendered PDF pages. The checked sub-review claims above are accurate; the numerical corrections concern errors in the published paper. Identification and generalizability assessments are reviewer judgments, not a reanalysis. The literature review’s external citation checks were not independently repeated and its source-specific criticisms are not relied on here.

- CONFIRMED — Methods/contribution: Table 2 gives −0.21 core and −0.02 total credits, approximately 18% extra-total-time student-years, and 0.96 total versus 0.06 core additional credits within that group (pp. 20–21); the denominator is student-years.
- CONFIRMED — Methods/contribution: Table 7’s preferred core-credit ELA coefficient is 0.022 SD (SE 0.008), with small, nonsignificant preferred math coefficients of 0.002 and 0.010 (p. 29).
- CONFIRMED — Writing: the narrative’s any-credit ELA estimate is “0.010 SD units” (p. 27), but the preferred Table 7 entry is “0.012” (p. 29); this guide uses the table value.
- CONFIRMED — Methods/writing: the preferred full-load odds ratios are 1.996 and 1.597, and the table note restricts these models to students whose full-load status changes (Table 6, p. 28); odds are not probabilities.
- CONFIRMED — Methods/contribution/writing: regular-diploma Matching 3 estimates are 1.133, 1.464*, and 1.792** for four-year any, four-year core, and five-year any exposure, respectively (Table 8, p. 30); its legend defines * p < .1 and ** p < .05 (p. 31).
- CONFIRMED — Writing/methods/reproducibility: “OR = 0.0464” and “88% lower” in the narrative (p. 32) disagree with “0.464” and “0.175” in Table 8 (pp. 30–31); calculations from the table yield 53.6% and 82.5% lower odds, respectively.
- CONFIRMED — Writing/reproducibility: Table 8’s continuation says “Four-year outcomes” (p. 31), while the narrative assigns its “OR = 0.175” to “after 5 years” (p. 32); sequence suggests a heading error but does not verify the intended horizon.
- CONFIRMED — Writing/reproducibility: “32,673 students (64,162 observations)” in the data section (p. 9) differs from “No. of students” = “32,685” and “No. of student-year observations” = “64,241” in Table 1 (p. 11); the supplied article does not reconcile them.
- CONFIRMED — Methods/writing/reproducibility: “student, grade, and school by year fixed effects” in the results (p. 25) differs from “grade by year and school fixed effects” added to student effects in Table 6’s note (p. 28); Equation 3 (p. 16) supports the latter documented specification.
- COULD NOT CHECK — Matching balance, assessment harmonization, and the combined-diploma null result depend on unavailable Supplementary Appendix Tables A2, A4, and A7 (referenced on pp. 13, 17–18, 29, 32); the main-text descriptions do not independently verify these results.

### Methods Review
**Rating:** Weak (high confidence)

The statewide administrative records provide useful descriptive evidence about EL-classified students’ relative course enrollment, and the student fixed-effects and matching analyses improve on unadjusted comparisons. However, the headline causal claims about course access are undermined by constructing the exposure from the same credits used as outcomes, while the graduation analysis remains vulnerable to selection through high-school persistence and diploma-track decisions. These are substantive identification problems, despite the paper’s appropriate qualifications of some causal interpretations.

**Strengths:**

- The administrative data link course enrollment, student characteristics, instructional experiences, assessments, and graduation outcomes. Comparing enrolled credits with non-EL peers in the same school, grade, and year provides a clear descriptive benchmark, and distinguishing total from core-subject enrollment is substantively useful (pp. 9, 12–14; Tables 1–2, pp. 10–11, 20–21).
- Student fixed effects address stable differences between students; grade-by-year and school effects address additional contextual variation; and the sequential specifications reveal how estimates change with adjustment. Student-clustered standard errors recognize repeated observations, and the fixed-effects logistic sample restriction to students whose full-load status changes is explicitly explained (pp. 16–17; Tables 6–7, pp. 28–29).
- The graduation analysis explicitly states common-support and conditional-independence assumptions, matches on substantively relevant demographic and prior-achievement measures, and avoids directly matching on subsequent reclassification. The authors acknowledge unsuccessful balance with alternative weighting methods and describe graduation estimates as exploratory rather than definitive (pp. 17–18, 29; Table 8, pp. 30–31).
- The paper acknowledges that credits enrolled do not establish credits earned or instructional quality, that fuller schedules can be mistaken for supplemental programming, and that summer and online records are incomplete. These disclosures help readers identify the descriptive estimand and its limits (pp. 12–13, 33–37; Table 4, p. 24).

**Weaknesses:**

- The exposure–outcome overlap is a central identification problem. Total-credit differential is constructed from the sum of enrolled subject credits, while Table 6 regresses those subject credits and full-course-load status on that differential. Using total rather than core credits does not remove the part–whole relationship acknowledged on p. 16. Positive subject-credit coefficients therefore partly describe how a larger total is composed; fixed effects do not turn this arithmetic association into an independently identified effect of providing extra instruction. Full-load status is not an exact identity, but it is also constructed from the same enrollment records (pp. 12, 14, 16; Table 6, p. 28).
- For achievement, student fixed effects do not remove changes in academic need, prior course failure, motivation, attendance, counseling, or diploma plans that can determine both enrollment and outcomes. The paper recognizes time-varying confounding, but the bound article contains no independent assignment mechanism or sensitivity analysis establishing that the available controls resolve it. Contemporaneous instructional controls may themselves be part of, or responses to, changing course exposure, so their inclusion is not necessarily a stronger estimate of the total effect (pp. 13–18; Table 7, p. 29).
- Graduation treatment is accumulated during high school rather than assigned at entry. Remaining enrolled gives students more opportunities to satisfy the exposure definition, while pursuing a regular rather than modified diploma can itself produce a fuller core schedule. Matching on observed characteristics does not separate these pathways from an effect of extra time. In addition, summed instructional experiences across high school are potentially post-treatment variables and proxies for duration of enrollment. These are live threats, not demonstrated estimates of the direction or size of bias (pp. 17–18, 33, 35–36; Table 8, pp. 30–31).
- The measure describes relative enrolled credits, not observed instructional minutes, attendance, instructional quality, or a uniform intervention. It can change because non-EL peers change their schedules even when an EL student’s own credits do not change. The “longer school day” classification is inferred from credit load and the absence of other recorded formats; it is not an independently measured extension of clock time. Similar under-reporting of summer courses across groups would not by itself eliminate individual exposure misclassification or bias from thresholding a noisy difference (pp. 12–14, 33–37; Table 4 and its note, p. 24).
- The main panel removes students after reclassification, and the within-student models depend on those with repeated usable observations. If course exposure or achievement influences reclassification, conditioning on continued EL status can select the observed achievement trajectories. The full-load estimates additionally apply to students whose outcome changes, as the table explicitly states. The graduation analysis instead follows an entry-defined EL cohort, so the outcome analyses do not identify effects for an identical population (pp. 9, 16–18; Table 6 note, p. 28).
- Precision and robustness remain incompletely established. Student clustering in the panel and heteroskedasticity-robust errors in the graduation models do not account for all possible school-level dependence from scheduling, shared peer benchmarks, or graduation practices. School fixed effects do not absorb school-specific changing shocks. The bound article does not report school-clustered sensitivity checks or multiplicity adjustment across the outcome and treatment families; marginal graduation findings deserve particular caution (pp. 16–18; Tables 6–8, pp. 28–31).
- Important execution details are delegated to unavailable online appendices: graduation balance and sample composition, assessment harmonization, alternative weighting results, and combined-diploma results cannot be independently assessed here. Table 8 uses different samples across diploma outcomes and follow-up horizons without a complete sample-flow explanation in the bound article, limiting interpretation of the estimates as a shift between diploma types (pp. 9, 13, 17–18, 29, 32; Table 8, pp. 30–31).

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Rely most on the descriptive conclusion that recorded core-course enrollment differs between current EL students and their local non-EL peers, and on the observed composition of fuller schedules. Interpret prevalence as a student-year measure of relative credit enrollment, not the proportion of distinct students ever offered an extra-time program (Tables 1–2 and 5, pp. 10–11, 20–21, 26).
- Read the course-taking coefficients as within-student enrollment associations with a built-in part–whole relationship. The full-load estimates are odds ratios, not changes in probability: the preferred middle- and high-school estimates are 1.996 and 1.597, respectively, and pertain to outcome-changing students (Table 6, p. 28). They do not establish how much an externally imposed increase in instructional time would improve access.
- The adjusted achievement associations are small: the preferred core-credit estimate for ELA is 0.022 SD with SE 0.008, while the preferred math estimates are 0.002 for total credits and 0.010 for core credits, each with SE 0.008 (Table 7, p. 29). Treat this as limited evidence of a small contemporaneous test-score relationship among observed students, not proof that additional instructional time cannot improve learning or that the instruction was low quality.
- Treat regular-diploma benefits as a hypothesis supported by selected observational comparisons. In the fully adjusted matched specification, the regular-diploma odds ratio for core extra time at the four-year horizon is 1.464 and is marked only at p < .1; the any-extra-time estimate at the five-year horizon is 1.792 and marked at p < .05 (Table 8, p. 30; significance key, p. 31). Neither is an absolute graduation-rate gain, and the table does not demonstrate that particular students switched from modified to regular diplomas.
- Before using the graduation estimates for policy projections, verify the unavailable balance tables, treatment and covariate timing, handling of dropout and incomplete follow-up, and the differing outcome-specific samples. Generalization should remain limited to comparable Oregon enrollment practices and observed EL populations; these estimates do not directly evaluate a specified summer, tutoring, or extended-day program (pp. 9, 17–18, 29, 33–37; Tables 4 and 8, pp. 24, 30–31).

**Detailed Commentary:**

Assessment basis: I read the complete bound article and checked the model equation and central exhibits against rendered PDF pages. Citations use the article’s printed page numbers. The online appendices are not bound into the supplied PDF and were unavailable for this assessment. Statements about definitions, specifications, and displayed estimates are document-verifiable; conclusions about identification and likely selection mechanisms are methodological judgments rather than a reanalysis of the data.

The principal issue is what the exposure represents. As defined on p. 12, the credit differential equals a student’s enrolled-credit total minus a contemporaneous local peer mean. Each subject-credit outcome is already part of that total. The authors recognize circularity for core-credit exposure on p. 16, but replacing it with all-subject exposure leaves every subject outcome inside the predictor. The regressions can reveal the allocation of fuller schedules across subjects, yet cannot independently establish that extra instructional provision caused that allocation. Similarly, more complete enrollment predicts the full-load indicator partly because both summarize the same schedule. This is more consequential than an ordinary residual-confounding caveat because it directly affects the paper’s claimed evidence for improved course access.

The achievement analysis is less mechanically compromised because test scores are separate outcomes. It nevertheless requires that changes in relative credits be conditionally unrelated to unobserved changes in achievement determinants. Current EL status, observed tests, changing course need, and the peer benchmark all complicate that interpretation. The main text standardizes scores within grade and year and acknowledges assessment changes, but its cross-assessment harmonization is in an unavailable appendix (p. 13). Standardization does not independently establish comparable constructs across tests. Missing assessment records also cannot all be interpreted as attrition, since the paper explicitly limits achievement analyses to tested grades (p. 16). The appropriate conclusion is that adjusted associations with measured achievement are small in the analyzed panel, with unresolved causal and measurement limitations.

The graduation design has a different and more demanding identification burden. Baseline covariate similarity is useful, but does not establish comparability of subsequent persistence, accumulated course failures, reclassification histories, or decisions about which diploma to pursue. The paper appropriately avoids matching directly on later reclassification while also including instructional experiences accumulated over high school (p. 18); those controls may themselves be downstream of earlier exposure. The label “doubly robust” on p. 18 is not established merely by combining CEM and outcome regression: the bound article does not demonstrate a formal guarantee that either model alone suffices, and neither approach removes unobserved confounding. Different diploma-specific estimation samples further prevent a straightforward interpretation of opposing coefficients as student-level substitution between diploma types (Table 8, pp. 30–31).

Several reporting issues are independently verifiable. For the panel specification, p. 25 describes “student, grade, and school by year fixed effects,” whereas the Table 6 note says “grade by year and school fixed effects” (p. 28), consistent with Equation 3 on p. 16. These are different controls; I interpret the equation and table note as the documented specification and do not credit the models with school-by-year adjustment. For modified diplomas, p. 32 prints “OR = 0.0464,” whereas the relevant fully adjusted Table 8 entry is “0.464” (p. 30). The table value implies approximately 54% lower odds, consistent with that part of the prose. However, p. 32 says “88% lower after 5 years,” whereas the associated table entry is “0.175” (Table 8, p. 31), implying 82.5% lower odds. There is also an unresolved horizon-label problem: the continuation panel on p. 31 is headed “Four-year outcomes,” while p. 32 explicitly associates “OR = 0.175” with “after 5 years”; its placement after the five-year panel on p. 30 supports, but does not verify, the latter interpretation. These discrepancies concern reporting, not proof that the underlying regressions were executed incorrectly, but readers should not repeat the prose values uncritically.

The weak rating is a judgment about the methods supporting the paper’s central positive causal conclusions, not a rejection of its descriptive contribution or of fixed effects and matching in general. The panel associations and exploratory graduation results are informative, and the authors disclose meaningful limitations. Nevertheless, the exposure–outcome overlap and unresolved timing and selection in the graduation design prevent the strongest claims about improved access and diploma attainment from carrying the causal weight assigned to them in the abstract and conclusion (pp. 1, 37).

### Literature Review
**Rating:** Adequate (high confidence)

The article offers a broad, interdisciplinary account of extra instructional time and English learners' access to coursework, drawing on quantitative evaluations, qualitative program studies, and research on educational inequality. Its positioning is generally useful, but the closest causal antecedent receives insufficient attention, a participation citation is summarized too selectively, and evidence from substantially different kinds of additional time is not always distinguished sharply enough. Readers should cite this study primarily for its statewide examination of relative credit enrollment among secondary EL-classified students, rather than as the introduction of causal research on extra time for this population.

**Strengths:**

- The review is organized around access, delivery format, instructional content, and outcomes for both the general population and EL-classified students (pp. 3–8). This structure makes the substantive gap legible: knowing that particular programs can help does not establish who receives additional credit-bearing instruction across a state or what that instruction covers.
- Coverage crosses disciplinary and methodological boundaries. The discussion connects sociological accounts of privately purchased enrichment and unequal opportunities with economics-of-education studies of instructional time, developmental research on organized activities, and qualitative accounts of newcomer and community-based programs (pp. 3–7). It also recognizes home-language development, identity, and belonging as educational aims rather than treating test performance as the only relevant outcome.
- The authors explicitly qualify several bodies of favorable evidence: they identify the absence of a formal comparison group in Arbreton et al., distinguish retention from the additional supports bundled with it, acknowledge conflicting participation findings, and discuss instructional quality and implementation constraints (pp. 5–7). The discussion also considers alternative explanations for limited achievement effects and possible harms from low-quality extra instruction (pp. 35–36). These are meaningful safeguards against a simple more-time-is-always-better narrative.
- The treatment of Kraft and Novicoff's distinction between total school time, instructional time, and active learning time is a useful interpretive framework (p. 35). The checked source supports the paper's broad account that average achievement benefits depend on dosage, use, and context. See [Kraft and Novicoff, Time in School](https://edworkingpapers.com/ai22-653).

**Weaknesses:**

- The closest antecedent is cited but not adequately differentiated. Page 7 summarizes Johnson (2020) as finding a positive effect on credit accumulation, then describes the existing EL literature as 'primarily descriptive and qualitative'; page 8 introduces the contribution as 'using causal methods to estimate the effects of extra time at the secondary level.' These statements are not necessarily contradictory, and the paper does not explicitly claim to be first. However, Johnson already used a difference-in-differences-in-differences design to study newcomer high school students' course taking, English proficiency, and graduation. Its graduation estimates were imprecise. That verified antecedent makes the new contribution principally broader population and statewide coverage, a different exposure measure, and additional outcome evidence—not the arrival of causal methods in this area. See [Johnson, Summer Credit Recovery Impact on Newcomer English Learners](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.3102/0002831219883237).
- The representation of Yu et al. (2015) is selectively positive. Page 6 places it among studies in which EL students or overlapping Latine and immigrant populations are 'equally or even over-represented in extra instructional opportunities.' The checked publisher abstract instead reports participation differences by ethnicity, immigrant-family background, and activity, including lower participation among Hispanic youth and comparable or higher participation for some non-Hispanic immigrant groups. This is mixed evidence within the same study, not a clean positive counterpart to the studies cited for underrepresentation. It also concerns organized out-of-school activities rather than an identified EL population receiving credit-bearing instruction. The article acknowledges overlapping populations, but readers should not repeat this citation as direct evidence of equitable access for EL-classified students. See [Yu, Newport-Berra, and Liu](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/josh.12255).
- The conceptual bridge between the reviewed interventions and the study's exposure remains incomplete. Retention, targeted tutoring, extended school days, summer enrichment, and extra subject periods alter different aspects of instruction (pp. 4–7); the present study measures credit enrollment relative to local non-EL peers (p. 12). The authors appropriately concede that this can reflect fuller schedules rather than supplemental offerings (pp. 33–34). My judgment is that evidence about deliberately designed programs therefore supplies context, but cannot by itself establish expected effects for this relative scheduling measure. This distinction limits how readers should interpret agreement or disagreement with the wider time-intervention literature.
- Engagement with conflicting evidence is real but could give readers a clearer account of how outcomes diverge. Although the paper cites Nomi and Allensworth (2009) and the Cortes studies, its reference list omits Nomi and Allensworth's later Sorting and Supporting. That study finds improved test performance alongside increased course failure among higher-skill students, with classroom sorting, relative standing, and pedagogy contributing to the pattern. It is especially pertinent to an article separating course access, tested learning, and educational attainment. Its omission does not invalidate the review, but leaves a useful mechanism-based counterexample undeveloped. See [Nomi and Allensworth (2013)](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.3102/0002831212469997).

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read Johnson (2020) alongside this article when citing evidence on additional instructional opportunities for secondary EL students. Distinguish a program-specific quasi-experiment involving newcomers from the present statewide analysis of relative course enrollment, and retain Johnson's uncertainty about graduation when describing the prior evidence.
- Use Kraft and Novicoff (2024) to distinguish scheduled exposure from active learning, and Nomi and Allensworth (2013) to understand why classroom organization can produce different effects on test scores and course success. These companion readings help situate the Oregon study at the intersection of instructional-time research and the sociology of course placement.
- Before repeating participation claims, check which population and activity each source actually measures. In particular, consult Yu et al.'s subgroup-specific findings rather than interpreting immigrant or Latine participation as an estimate of EL-classified students' access to public credit-bearing instruction.
- For the paper's substantive lineage, pair its statewide account with the already-cited Callahan (2005) and Umansky et al. (2024) on curricular access, and with the community-based education literature discussed on p. 7. Credit-bearing schedules are an important part of multilingual students' opportunities, but do not encompass the cultural, linguistic, and developmental opportunities covered by that broader literature.

**Detailed Commentary:**

The adequate rating reflects substantial relevant coverage and genuine engagement with qualifications, together with identifiable problems of precision and comparative positioning. The paper is not missing an entire disciplinary perspective: sociology, economics, developmental research, language education, and qualitative scholarship are all represented. Nor would a longer reference list alone resolve the main issues. The central reader-facing task is to distinguish evidence about instructional quantity from evidence about program design, course allocation, and instructional quality.

The strongest defensible novelty claim is the attempt to describe formal credit-bearing exposure across a statewide secondary EL population without starting from one named intervention. The article itself explains both the gain in scope and the resulting loss of information about instructional intent and content (pp. 12, 33–34). My assessment is that this is a meaningful contribution, but the paper should be read as extending an established course-access and extra-time literature. Its coverage of Johnson is broadly compatible with that study's positive course-taking finding, yet does not convey how closely the earlier research already overlaps with the present causal question and outcome domains.

Verification limits: I read the complete supplied article, including its references. External checks used primary publication abstracts or the authors' working-paper record for Johnson, Yu et al., Nomi and Allensworth, and Kraft and Novicoff; they establish the specific comparisons above, not a comprehensive audit of every cited study. Claims about the article's coverage and wording are document-verifiable; judgments about the importance of omissions, the strength of novelty, and transferability across forms of time are interpretive assessments. I do not claim exhaustive knowledge of this subfield. Online supplements and appendices were not available in the supplied paper and were not inspected; no conclusion here depends on their presumed contents.

### Writing Review
**Rating:** Weak (high confidence)

The article has a clear question-driven structure and explains its central instructional-time measure accessibly, but repeated numerical, labeling, and interpretive inconsistencies make the prose unsafe to quote without checking the exhibits. The broad contrast between course-access findings and limited achievement gains is conveyed well; the graduation findings and headline causal language require substantially more caution than the abstract supplies.

**Strengths:**

- Organization is effective: the research questions on p. 3 recur in the methods and findings headings, separating who receives extra time, its formats and uses, and estimated outcomes. Tables 2–5 carry the descriptive argument (pp. 20–26), while Tables 6–8 carry the outcome argument (pp. 28–31). Readers can readily locate the evidence relevant to a particular question.
- The central measurement explanation on pp. 12–14 is unusually useful. It distinguishes enrolled credits from a directly observed time intervention, defines the local non-EL comparison group, separates any-subject from core-content measures, and illustrates how supplemental enrollment and missing core coursework can coexist. The discussion of fuller schedules on pp. 33–34 and the limitations on pp. 36–37 further clarify what the administrative measure can and cannot mean.
- Important qualifications are present in the body. The methods identify threats from unobserved changing circumstances and describe the graduation estimates as tentative (pp. 17–18); the graduation results explicitly call themselves exploratory (p. 29). The discussion considers alternative explanations for limited test-score gains and acknowledges that instructional quality and successful credit completion are unobserved (pp. 35–37).
- Several exhibit notes provide substantial interpretive help. Table 3 identifies reference groups and distinguishes odds ratios from credit coefficients (pp. 22–23); Table 4 defines the format categories (p. 24); and Table 6 explains why the full-load models use a smaller, changing-status sample than the credit-enrollment models (p. 28). The reported core-credit sums in the course-taking narrative agree with the preferred-model entries in Table 6 (p. 27 and Table 6, p. 28).

**Weaknesses:**

- Verified graduation-number errors: p. 32 reports '54% lower' odds with 'OR = 0.0464', whereas the relevant modified-diploma, core-time, Matching 3 cell is '0.464' (Table 8, p. 30). Calculating from the table gives a 53.6% reduction, consistent with the percentage but not the prose's decimal placement. The same paragraph reports '88% lower after 5 years (OR = 0.175)'; Table 8's corresponding Matching 3 cell is also '0.175' (p. 31), which implies an 82.5% reduction, not 88%. These are errors in the published PDF, not extraction artifacts.
- Verified outcome-label conflict in the principal graduation exhibit: Table 8 begins its later-outcome block with 'Five-year outcomes' on p. 30, but the continuation containing the core-time estimates is headed 'Four-year outcomes' on p. 31. The narrative identifies the modified-diploma estimate 'OR = 0.175' as occurring 'after 5 years' (p. 32; Table 8, p. 31). The sequence and narrative suggest a continuation-header error, but the document does not resolve it explicitly. Table 8 also labels its sample counts 'No. of student-year observations' (pp. 30–31), while the graduation-data description says it 'condensed students’ full high school enrollment into a single observation' (p. 9). Readers must reconcile the outcome horizon and observational unit themselves.
- Verified sample-description disagreements: the data section gives '32,673 students (64,162 observations)' (p. 9), whereas Table 1 reports 'No. of students' as '32,685' and 'No. of student-year observations' as '64,241' (p. 11). Table 2 also gives the total as '64,241' (p. 20), without explaining the difference from the methods. Likewise, Table 1's title dates the sample 'from 2013–14 to 2018–19' (p. 10), but Table 5's note says 'from 2012–13 to 2018–19' (p. 26). These discrepancies leave the exact descriptive sample and time coverage unclear.
- Verified achievement and specification discrepancies: the ELA any-credit result is described as '0.010 SD units' on p. 27, but Table 7's preferred Model 3 entry is '0.012' (p. 29). Both presentations describe a nonsignificant result, so this does not reverse the substantive conclusion. More consequentially for identifying the fitted model, p. 25 says the preferred specification includes 'student, grade, and school by year fixed effects', whereas Table 6's note says the base model contains student effects and the next model 'adds grade by year and school fixed effects' (p. 28; also Table 7, p. 29). Equation 3's accompanying description agrees with the table notes (p. 16). These are different specifications, and readers should not silently treat the prose descriptions as interchangeable.
- Odds are sometimes narrated as probabilities. The statement that additional time 'doubled a given student’s likelihood of being enrolled in a full course load' (p. 27) is supported by a row explicitly labeled 'Full academic load (odds ratio)', with preferred-model estimate '1.996' (Table 6, p. 28). That is approximately doubled odds, not doubled probability. The table supplies no baseline probability from which a probability change could be calculated. Its note also restricts the logistic estimates to students whose full-load status changes, a qualification absent from that broad prose formulation.
- In my judgment, abstract fidelity is materially weakened by uneven calibration. The abstract says extra time 'substantially increased the likelihood' of full-course enrollment and regular-diploma graduation (p. 1), while the graduation section says 'We consider these results exploratory' (p. 29). Table 8 shows a mixed regular-diploma pattern: the preferred four-year any-time estimate is '1.133' without a significance marker, the core-time estimate is '1.464*', and the five-year any-time estimate is '1.792**' (p. 30); the legend distinguishes '* p < .1' from '** p < .05' (p. 31). The abstract accurately identifies Oregon, descriptive and quasi-experimental methods, and limited achievement effects, but omits the local credit-relative definition, the differing outcome samples and treatments, and the tentative graduation interpretation. It also omits the body's report of no statistically significant combined-diploma result (p. 32, attributed there to unavailable Supplementary Table A7). That last claim can be reported as the authors' account, not independently checked from the supplied exhibits.
- The discussion blurs distinct subgroup results. It says 'newcomer students, long-term ELs, and ELs with disabilities all more likely to receive extra time' (p. 33), but Table 3 reports 'Long-term' any-time odds of '0.958' and core-time odds of '1.244***', while 'Dually identified' students have any-time odds of '1.241**' and core-time odds of '0.751**' (p. 22). Thus the generalization does not hold for a common adjusted outcome across those groups. In a related interpretive overreach, p. 19 describes the '−0.28 intercept' as showing the EL population's overall deficit and p. 21 says 'No subgroup fully closed the core content credit gap'. Table 3 labels those quantities 'Intercept' (p. 22), with explicit reference categories and additional continuous covariates (pp. 22–23). My judgment is that an intercept and isolated subgroup coefficients cannot establish those population-wide or all-profile statements; Table 2 supplies the directly interpretable descriptive averages instead (pp. 20–21).
- Table 1 is not self-contained about graduation denominators. Under 'Mean (all ELs)', it lists 'Graduation rate (5 year) (%)' as '0.15' and 'Received regular diploma (5 year) (%)' as '0.16'; under students without extra time, the same rows are '0.13' and '0.15' (p. 11). A regular-diploma component should not exceed an all-diploma total if denominators and outcome definitions are shared. The table gives no row-specific denominator explanation, so this is an unresolved reporting inconsistency rather than proof of a particular corrected value. More generally, percentage-labeled rows in Tables 1–2 display proportions, requiring a unit conversion before quotation (pp. 10–11, 20–21).
- The home-language description does not match the displayed categories. The methods list 'Spanish, Vietnamese, Arabic, Russian, and Chinese' (p. 13), but Tables 1–3 instead display 'English' alongside Chinese, Spanish, Vietnamese, Russian, and Other, with no separate Arabic category (Table 1, p. 10; Table 2, p. 20; Table 3, p. 22). Table 1's note also calls these the 'top five non-English languages' (p. 11). Readers cannot determine from the supplied document whether the prose or the category labels describe the intended coding.
- Some substantive labels invite stronger interpretations than their definitions warrant. The results say students received extra time 'through a longer school day' (p. 24), whereas Table 4 defines that category through higher enrolled credits during a term and absence of other identified formats (p. 24). The discussion later says such students may 'simply' have had 'fuller high school schedules' (p. 33). These are compatible only if readers recognize that longer day is an inferred administrative category, not verified clock time. Similarly, 'displaced core content' is defined by missing a core subject despite extra enrollment (p. 14), not by demonstrating that extra instruction caused the omission. The results' explanation that students 'never enrolled in an ELA, math, science, or social studies course that year' (p. 25) is ambiguous beside the clearer definition 'lacking one or more of the four core content area classes' (p. 14).
- The density is manageable, but important interpretive burdens sit outside the main narrative. The wide, rotated Tables 3, 5, and 8 require deliberate reading, and significance-star conventions change across the outcome tables (Tables 6–8, pp. 28–31). The online appendices hold matching balance, assessment harmonization, combined-diploma results, and some allocation results. They are not bound into the supplied PDF and were unavailable for this review; the main-text summaries cannot substitute for inspecting those exhibits. This limits the reader's ability to resolve the paper's reporting inconsistencies.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- For a short but responsible reading, prioritize the measurement definitions on pp. 12–14, the causal qualifications and distinct graduation design on pp. 16–18, Tables 2 and 4–8, and the fuller-schedules and limitations discussions on pp. 33–37. The broad literature overview on pp. 3–7 and the opening discussion recap on pp. 32–33 can be skimmed once the question is clear.
- Before quoting graduation findings, read Table 8 across both pages with its legend (pp. 30–31), then check p. 32. Preserve the distinction between odds and probabilities, regular and modified diplomas, any and core extra time, and the alternative follow-up horizons. Flag the continuation heading and corrected arithmetic explicitly rather than copying the narrative percentages.
- Use Table 2 for descriptive prevalence and average credit gaps (pp. 20–21), Table 3 for conditional subgroup comparisons (pp. 22–23), and Table 6 for within-student outcome estimates (p. 28). Do not substitute the regression intercept for an overall mean or combine subgroup conclusions from the any-time and core-time columns.
- Read 'extra instructional time' as a relative enrolled-credit measure and 'electives' as the paper's broad residual category, which also includes graduation requirements (pp. 12, 34, and note 3 on p. 38). Keep the descriptive differences between students in Table 5 (p. 26) separate from the within-student estimates in Table 6 (p. 28) when interpreting how additional enrollment is distributed across subjects.
- Do not quote Table 1's graduation rates or a definitive sample total without noting the unresolved denominator and sample-count inconsistencies (pp. 9–11). Treat statements attributed only to online appendices as unverified here, particularly the combined-diploma conclusion on p. 32. Read the abstract alongside the exploratory qualification on p. 29 before summarizing the strength of the graduation evidence.

**Detailed Commentary:**

This assessment concerns exposition and fidelity to the published evidence, not an independent reanalysis or a full methods review. I read the complete article, including notes and references, and inspected rendered PDF exhibits to check the numerical and labeling problems described above. The errors in the displayed graduation narrative, continuation heading, sample counts, and achievement coefficient are document-verifiable; the judgments about abstract overstatement, intercept interpretation, and ambiguous substantive labels are interpretive assessments grounded in the cited passages.

The weak rating reflects the accumulation of problems in material that readers are likely to cite, especially the headline graduation claim. It does not mean the article is generally unreadable or that its findings have been disproved. Its structure is sound, many definitions are careful, and the main achievement interpretation survives the small coefficient discrepancy. The problem is that a reader must repeatedly reconstruct the intended meaning from tables, methods, and later qualifications, and some ambiguities remain unresolved even after doing so.

The abstract's rough prevalence description is consistent with Table 2's student-year tabulation (pp. 20–21), but that denominator and the relative-credit threshold become clear only in the body. Its account of limited standardized-achievement benefits is also consistent with the preferred estimates in Table 7 (p. 29). The weakest compression occurs when the abstract joins course-load and graduation findings into a single confident causal statement despite the different designs and the body's explicit reservations. Readers can recover a more qualified account from the full text, but an abstract-only reading gives a firmer impression than the reported evidence warrants.

### Contribution Review
**Rating:** Adequate (high confidence)

The paper contributes a useful statewide account of relative credit-bearing course exposure among secondary students classified as English learners in Oregon, extending the program-specific evidence described in its literature review. Its strongest addition is evidence about the distribution and subject composition of course access; its findings on achievement and diploma type are informative but do not establish that a defined expansion of instructional time would produce the advertised benefits. In my judgment, this is a meaningful, bounded contribution to an important equity question rather than definitive evidence for an instructional-time policy.

**Strengths:**

- The substantive extension is clear. As the paper describes prior research, Johnson's summer-credit-recovery study already supplied evidence concerning newcomers, while other studies examined particular programs or elementary retention policies (pp. 6–8). This paper broadens the population and examines ordinary course schedules across a state, connecting access, subject allocation, achievement, and diploma type. The novelty is chiefly the scope and operationalization of exposure, rather than a new causal method or discovery that additional instruction can matter.
- The descriptive results separate overall course exposure from core-content access in a policy-relevant way. Table 2 reports extra total enrollment in 18% of EL student-year observations, alongside average differentials of −0.02 total credits and −0.21 core credits relative to local non-EL peers (p. 20, Table 2). Among observations classified as receiving extra total time, the corresponding differentials are 0.96 total credits but only 0.06 core credits (p. 21, Table 2). These verified patterns show why identifying fuller schedules does not by itself establish substantially greater access to core instruction.
- Examining subject allocation and diploma type adds information beyond a generic test-score evaluation. Electives account for the largest reported enrollment difference between EL students with and without extra total time (p. 26, Table 5), and the authors explain that this category includes graduation requirements as well as enrichment (p. 38, note 3). In my judgment, distinguishing course opportunity, measured achievement, and diploma pathways is valuable even when the causal interpretation remains uncertain.
- The paper offers substantial interpretive qualifications: it acknowledges possible unobserved confounding, describes the graduation estimates as exploratory, discusses fuller schedules as an alternative to specialized supplemental programs, and identifies missing information on credit completion and instructional quality (pp. 17–18, 29, 33–37). Those qualifications allow a careful reader to extract a defensible contribution.

**Weaknesses:**

- The central measure identifies relative enrolled credits, not additional instructional minutes or receipt of a specified intervention (p. 12). A student's differential can change when the peer benchmark changes, and fuller schedules can reflect unmet requirements or repeated coursework rather than supplemental provision (pp. 33–36). The 'longer school day' category is inferred from course enrollment and the absence of other identified formats, rather than directly observed clock time (p. 24, Table 4 note). My judgment is that this limits the paper's value as evidence about extending school days, even while preserving its value as evidence about relative course exposure.
- Course-taking results partly relate components of enrolled credits to a predictor constructed from total enrolled credits (pp. 12, 16; p. 28, Table 6). This makes the composition of additional enrollment informative, but the positive relationship with course access is not independent confirmation that an externally imposed increase in time causes access to improve. Student fixed effects also leave time-varying selection unresolved, as the paper acknowledges (p. 17).
- The most consequential policy claim, improved regular-diploma attainment, rests on matching students whose exposure accumulates during high school (pp. 17–18). Continued enrollment, graduation plans, and changing academic circumstances could influence both accumulated exposure and diploma outcomes. Table 8's fully adjusted matched estimates for extra time in any subject are 1.133 for regular graduation within four years, without a significance marker, and 1.792 within five years, significant at p < .05 (pp. 30–31, Table 8 and its significance key). This is suggestive evidence about diploma pathways, not a stable causal effect on graduation generally.
- Statewide coverage strengthens the Oregon description but does not establish national representativeness. The primary panel follows students while currently EL-classified, whereas the graduation sample follows students classified at high-school entry even if subsequently reclassified (p. 9). Oregon's diploma structure, local peer benchmarks, incomplete summer and online records, and the pre-pandemic observation period limit transfer to other populations and contemporary programs (pp. 8–13; pp. 10–11, Table 1; pp. 33–37).

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Cite this paper for Oregon evidence on relative credit-bearing course exposure, its distribution among EL students, and the distinction between fuller schedules and core-content access. Describe the prevalence measure as student-year exposure under a local comparison rule, not the share of students nationally offered a supplemental program (pp. 20–21, Table 2).
- Cite the achievement findings narrowly: in the preferred model, an additional core-credit differential is associated with 0.022 SD higher ELA achievement, while the other reported preferred-model estimates are small and not statistically significant (p. 29, Table 7). This does not show that all forms of additional instruction are ineffective or that students gained no learning beyond what these assessments measured.
- For graduation, use language such as 'exploratory matched evidence linking extra course exposure to diploma type.' Do not translate odds ratios into equivalent percentage changes in graduation probability or cite the study as establishing higher overall completion. The authors report no statistically significant combined-diploma result on p. 32, referring to Supplementary Appendix Table A7; that appendix is unavailable here, so this combined-outcome statement is author-reported rather than independently verified.
- Do not use the paper to rank summer school, online instruction, longer days, or fuller schedules by effectiveness, or to establish that fuller schedules are cost-effective. The study cannot separate these interventions adequately and does not estimate their comparative costs (pp. 24, 33–37).
- Readers should regard the main open questions as which changes to schedules actually increase useful instruction, whether enrolled courses are completed, how instructional quality and EL-service organization affect outcomes, and whether diploma differences translate into postsecondary benefits. These remain unresolved rather than demonstrated mechanisms (pp. 33–37).

**Detailed Commentary:**

My assessment distinguishes the documented contribution from its policy interpretation. The document supports a broad description of relative enrollment and an observational comparison of outcomes. The important conceptual update is that routine scheduling may be an overlooked source of differences in instructional opportunity, and that additional overall enrollment need not resolve core-content exclusion. That insight is useful for researchers and practitioners without requiring the causal claims to be definitive. It extends the access problem established in earlier work described by the authors; it does not establish that problem for the first time.

The most quotable claims are stronger than the paper's most secure contribution. The abstract says extra time 'substantially increased the likelihood of their enrolling in a full course load and graduating with a regular diploma' (p. 1), whereas the graduation results explicitly say, 'We consider these results exploratory' (p. 29). These statements differ in evidentiary emphasis: my judgment is that readers should carry the latter qualification into every citation of the former. Similarly, diploma-type differences do not demonstrate individual students switching diploma pathways, and limited test-score associations do not diagnose instructional quality.

Relative to the literature as summarized in the paper, this is a useful broad observational reference for secondary EL course exposure. It complements focused intervention studies rather than superseding them as the best causal evidence on additional instructional time. I have not independently assessed the cited studies or established a comprehensive literature ranking. The unavailable online appendices contain matching diagnostics, alternative estimates, and combined-diploma results that matter for assessing the strongest claims; their contents cannot be presumed verified from the main article's descriptions.

The authors are generally candid about measurement and identification limits, although the abstract and conclusion give readers less qualified causal language than the methods and graduation sections. The contribution warrants an adequate rating because its descriptive scope and policy-relevant distinctions add knowledge, while the heterogeneous exposure measure and uncertain causal interpretation limit how much it should change expectations about a particular policy. The strongest practical use is to motivate closer examination of scheduling and course access, not to prescribe a proven intervention.

### Reproducibility Review
**Rating:** Weak (high confidence)

The article identifies its administrative data provider and explains the main exposure measures, outcomes, and modeling strategies, making the broad analysis understandable. However, the supplied paper provides neither a documented data-access pathway nor replication code, and consequential sample-construction, harmonization, and estimation details are missing or deferred to unavailable supplements. Unresolved sample and specification discrepancies further prevent reliable reproduction of the central results from the available report.

**Strengths:**

- Data provenance and broad eligibility are clear: the study uses longitudinal Oregon Department of Education administrative records, distinguishes the current-EL panel from the graduation cohort, and explains how reclassification affects inclusion in each analysis (p. 9; p. 38, note 2). The institutional partnership and acknowledgment identify the actual data provider (pp. 9, 37).
- The central exposure is described operationally: enrolled credits are compared with non-EL peers in the same school, grade, and year, with separate all-subject and core-subject versions and continuous and binary measures. The paper explains course-duration eligibility and credit scaling, while the descriptive-table note restates the binary exposure definition (p. 12; Table 2, p. 21). Table 4 supplies useful operational definitions of summer, online, concurrent, and longer-day enrollment rather than leaving every format definition solely to the supplement (p. 24).
- Equations and accompanying text identify the principal regressions, fixed effects, broad covariate groups, and variance estimators. The graduation analysis lists exact-matching variables, the coarsening approach for English proficiency, and use of matching weights; it also distinguishes annual exposure in the panel from cumulative exposure in the graduation analysis (pp. 15–18, Equations 1–4).
- The main regression tables report exposure estimates, standard errors, sample sizes, and progressively adjusted specifications (Tables 3 and 6–8, pp. 22–23, 28–31). Table 6 explicitly explains why the fixed-effects logistic full-load models retain only students whose outcome changes, helping readers interpret their smaller estimation samples (p. 28). The authors also disclose likely underreporting of summer and online coursework and the absence of information on whether enrolled credits were earned (pp. 12–13, 36).

**Weaknesses:**

- The supplied article names ODE as the source but gives no application procedure, data-use-agreement pathway, access contact, or data-availability statement. It also supplies no replication-package location, posted analysis code, software/version information, or executable example (data discussion, p. 9; disclosures and notes, pp. 37–38). These are findings about the supplied article, not evidence that no access mechanism or code exists elsewhere. Protecting student records is legitimate; the reproducibility problem is the lack of a documented route and shareable computational materials.
- Rebuilding the analytic records would require consequential guesses. The report does not supply the course-code crosswalk, file-linkage and duplicate-record rules, assignment of a single school/grade to mobile or concurrently enrolled students, or a complete recipe for translating heterogeneous course dates into credits and assigning summer records to academic years (pp. 9, 12, 15; Table 4, p. 24). The population used to standardize scores and the complete assessment-harmonization rules are not given in the main text; the latter are explicitly deferred to Supplementary Appendix Table A4 (p. 13). Those choices affect both the exposure and the achievement analyses.
- Sample accounting is incomplete and internally inconsistent. The data section reports “32,673 students (64,162 observations)” (p. 9), whereas Table 1 reports “No. of students” as “32,685” and “No. of student-year observations” as “64,241” (p. 11). Table 3 then reports “53311” student-year observations (p. 23), without a reconciliation of exclusions or missing-data treatment that produces this estimation sample. The explanation of outcome switching in Table 6 deserves credit, but it does not provide a complete sample-flow account for the other model families (p. 28).
- The headline panel specification is not entirely unambiguous. The results describe the preferred model as including “student, grade, and school by year fixed effects” (p. 25), whereas the Table 6 note says “grade by year and school fixed effects,” alongside student effects (p. 28); the latter agrees with the explanation of Equation 3 (p. 16). These are different specifications. In addition, the panel-model covariate lists use “such as,” and the article does not provide an exhaustive model-by-model variable list, commands, or rules for missing covariates and singleton observations (pp. 13–16).
- Graduation reproducibility depends especially heavily on unavailable material. The paper describes matching and weighted regression, but the pre/post-match distributions are deferred to Supplementary Appendix Table A2, the alternative weighting analysis to A5, and combined-diploma results to A7 (pp. 17–18, 29, 32). Exact coarsening cutpoints, handling of missing English-proficiency scores, treated/control counts by estimation sample, weight construction/normalization, and outcome-specific exclusions cannot be recovered from the main report. Table 8 provides estimates and standard errors but does not reconcile its differing samples across diploma outcomes or explain why its unmatched and matched columns use the same displayed sample counts within each outcome block (pp. 30–31).

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Before attempting replication, request the ODE access requirements and source-file inventory, the analysis scripts and software versions, the course-code and assessment crosswalks, and a sample-flow record from source records through each reported model. Prioritize reconstruction of the non-EL comparison means, mobile-student school assignment, summer-year allocation, and treatment accumulation after EL reclassification.
- For the panel findings, reconcile the text/Table 1 sample counts and identify the exact exclusions behind each regression table. Confirm which fixed-effects structure was actually estimated and obtain the complete covariate and missing-data rules. With authorized data access, reproduce the descriptive credit measures before attempting the course-taking and achievement estimates (Tables 1–3 and 6–7, pp. 10–11, 20–23, 28–29).
- For the graduation findings, obtain the unavailable matching diagnostics and combined-diploma tables, plus the coarsening cutpoints, weights, treatment/control sample counts, and estimation logs. Verify the outcome horizons and reconcile narrative/table discrepancies before using the reported magnitudes; neither the claimed quality of balance nor the combined-diploma conclusion is independently checkable from the supplied PDF (pp. 17–18, 29–32; Table 8, pp. 30–31).

**Detailed Commentary:**

This assessment concerns the supplied article and its extracted text, including visual inspection of relevant tables and footnotes. The online appendices are not bound into the PDF and are unavailable for this review. Their cited contents may resolve some gaps, so an unavailable diagnostic is not treated as proof that the authors never performed it. No external repository or administrative-data access process was independently verified.

The report supports an informed reconstruction of the design, but not an exact reconstruction of the analysis. A researcher could understand why within-student models and a separate matched graduation analysis were used, and could inspect reported directions, uncertainty, and sensitivity to added controls. Recreating the underlying records, reproducing exclusions, checking the claimed matching balance, and regenerating the estimates would still require additional materials. This distinction is particularly important because the credit differential is a constructed measure: choices about course coding, enrollment duration, comparison students, and school assignment can change the treatment before any regression is run.

There are also directly verifiable problems with the graduation reporting. Table 8 labels its continuation block “Four-year outcomes” (p. 31), yet the discussion identifies the modified-diploma result from that block as “after 5 years (OR = 0.175, p < .001)” (p. 32; corresponding Table 8, p. 31, Matching 3 estimate “0.175”). Separately, the discussion prints “OR = 0.0464” for the earlier modified-diploma result (p. 32), whereas Table 8 prints “0.464” (p. 30, core-time, modified-diploma Matching 3 column). These are document-level discrepancies, not proof of incorrect underlying estimation; identifying the intended horizon and estimate requires clarification or the original outputs.

My judgment is therefore weak rather than insufficient: substantial measurement and model documentation exists, and the principal estimates are exposed to scrutiny. The rating is not a penalty for withholding confidential student data. It reflects the combined effect of an undocumented access route, absent computational materials, incomplete preprocessing and sample accounting, unavailable diagnostic evidence, and contradictory specification/reporting details that materially obstruct verification of the central findings. Confidence is high about these limits in the supplied document, not about what might be recoverable from unavailable supplements or author-held files.
